solution:
**Zinc.**

The bracket offers only two metals, zinc and copper, and this chapter's own displacement work rules copper out. The chapter opens with the reaction 'on adding zinc dust to blue coloured copper sulphate solution, a colourless solution of zinc sulphate is formed' — that is, \(\text{CuSO}_4(aq) + \text{Zn}(s) \rightarrow \text{ZnSO}_4(aq) + \text{Cu}(s)\) — and it defines a displacement reaction as one 'in which the place of the ion of a less reactive element in a compound is taken by another more reactive element'. So copper is the **less** reactive of the pair; a copper layer would be the wrong way round and could not protect iron. Zinc is the reactive metal of the two, so the layer applied on iron sheets is a layer of zinc.

[Note: this chapter does not itself describe a protective metal coating. It ends the corrosion section with 'Corrosion is a very serious problem. We are going to study about it in the metallurgy chapter', and the reactivity series that would rank zinc against iron is taught there, not here. The reasoning above is the most this chapter supports on its own.]

**Oxidation.**

Ferrous sulphate is \(\text{FeSO}_4\) and ferric sulphate is \(\text{Fe}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3\), so the change is

\(2\text{FeSO}_4 \rightarrow \text{Fe}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3\)

and the chapter reduces it to the net ionic reaction \(\text{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{3+}\) (ferrous to ferric). Its reason is given in full: 'When ferric ion is formed from ferrous ion the positive charge is increased by one unit. While this happens the ferrous ion loses one electron', and 'oxidation means losing one or more electrons.' Losing an electron and gaining positive charge is oxidation, so the conversion of ferrous sulphate to ferric sulphate is an oxidation reaction. The chapter shows it happening in reaction (25), where \(\text{KMnO}_4\) in the presence of acid oxidises \(\text{FeSO}_4\) to \(\text{Fe}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3\).

**Electrolysis.**

The chapter states it directly: 'water decomposes into hydrogen and oxygen gases on passing electric current through acidulated water. This decomposition takes place by means of electrical energy. Therefore it is called electrolysis.' The equation given is

\(2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \xrightarrow{\text{Electrical energy}} 2\text{H}_2\uparrow + \text{O}_2\uparrow\)

[Note: 'decomposition' also stands in the bracket and is not wrong in itself — this **is** a decomposition reaction, one reactant giving two products. But the chapter keeps a separate, narrower name for the case where the decomposition is driven by electricity, which is exactly the condition this statement names, so 'electrolysis' is the answer the blank is asking for and 'decomposition' is the distractor.]

**Double displacement.**

The chapter's definition is 'The reaction in which the ions in the reactants are exchanged to form a precipitate is a double displacement reaction.' Here the barium and zinc ions change partners with the chloride and sulphate ions:

\(\text{BaCl}_2(aq) + \text{ZnSO}_4(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4\downarrow + \text{ZnCl}_2(aq)\)

The white precipitate is barium sulphate — this same exercise gives those products in the Q.9 matching table. Because two ions are exchanged (not one element displacing another) and an insoluble solid separates out, it is a double displacement reaction, exactly like the chapter's own example \(\text{AgNO}_3(aq) + \text{NaCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgCl}\downarrow + \text{NaNO}_3(aq)\), in which 'a white precipitate of silver chloride is formed by an exchange of silver and sodium ions present in the reactants.'

It is called a **redox reaction**.

The chapter puts it as an equation of names: 'Redox Reaction = Reduction + Oxidation', arrived at because 'oxidation and reduction reactions occur simultaneously. The reductant is oxidized by the oxidant and the oxidant is reduced by the reductant. Due to this characteristics of the reduction and oxidation reactions, a single term 'redox reaction' is used in place of the two terms.'

**Example** — passing hydrogen gas over black copper oxide, when 'a reddish coloured layer of copper is formed':

\(\text{CuO} + \text{H}_2 \rightarrow \text{Cu} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

The chapter explains this example itself: 'an oxygen atom goes away from CuO (copper oxide), which means that reduction of copper oxide takes place, whereas hydrogen molecule takes up oxygen atom and water \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) is formed meaning, oxidation of hydrogen takes place.' So \(\text{CuO}\) is reduced and \(\text{H}_2\) is oxidised in one and the same reaction — \(\text{H}_2\) is the reductant and \(\text{CuO}\) the oxidant.

The decomposition of hydrogen peroxide is

\(2\text{H}_2\text{O}_2(l) \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) + \text{O}_2\uparrow\)

and the chapter says it 'takes place slowly at room temperature'. Its rate is increased **by adding a catalyst — manganese dioxide (\(\text{MnO}_2\)) powder**: 'the same reaction occurs at a faster rate on adding manganese dioxide \((\text{MnO}_2)\) powder in it.'

A catalyst is defined in the chapter as 'The substance in whose presence the rate of a chemical reaction increases, without causing any chemical change to it' — so the \(\text{MnO}_2\) speeds the reaction up and is itself left unchanged, and only a small quantity is needed.

The chapter lists four other factors that decide the rate of a reaction — the nature of the reactants, the size of the reactant particles, the concentration of the reactants and the temperature — and of these, raising the temperature and using a more concentrated solution of hydrogen peroxide would also increase the rate. But the catalyst is the method the chapter names for this particular reaction.

The chapter defines both terms together: 'The substances taking part in chemical reaction are called **reactants**, whereas the substances formed as a result of a chemical reaction by formation of new bonds are called **products**.' In a chemical equation the reactants are written on the left hand side and the products on the right, with an arrow between them pointing towards the products.

**Example 1** (the chapter's own): 'formation of carbon dioxide gas by combustion of coal in air is a chemical reaction. In this reaction coal (carbon) and oxygen (from air) are the reactants while carbon dioxide is the product.'

\(\text{C} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{CO}_2\)

**Example 2**: \(\text{CuSO}_4(aq) + \text{Zn}(s) \rightarrow \text{ZnSO}_4(aq) + \text{Cu}(s)\)

Here copper sulphate and zinc are the reactants; zinc sulphate and copper are the products. As the chapter notes, the products have 'totally different properties' from the reactants — the ionic bond in the reactant \(\text{CuSO}_4\) breaks and a new ionic bond is formed in the product \(\text{ZnSO}_4\).

With reference to oxygen and hydrogen the chapter defines two types of reaction, oxidation and reduction.

**Oxidation** — 'The chemical reaction in which a reactant combines with oxygen or loses hydrogen to form the product is called oxidation reaction.' So there are two ways a reactant can be oxidised:

- by gaining oxygen: \(2\text{Mg} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MgO}\) and \(\text{C} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{CO}_2\)
- by losing hydrogen: \(\text{MgH}_2 \rightarrow \text{Mg} + \text{H}_2\) and \(\text{CH}_3\text{-CH}_3 \rightarrow \text{CH}_2\text{=CH}_2 + \text{H}_2\)

**Reduction** — 'The chemical reactions in which reactants gain hydrogen are called reduction reactions. Similarly, the reaction in which a reactant loses oxygen to form the product is also called reduction reaction.' Again two ways:

- by gaining hydrogen: vegetable oil \((l) + \text{H}_2(g) \rightarrow\) vanaspati ghee \((s)\), carried out at \(60\ ^\circ\text{C}\) over a nickel catalyst
- by losing oxygen: \(\text{CuO} + \text{H}_2 \rightarrow \text{Cu} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\), in which copper oxide loses its oxygen

The two never happen apart. In the last equation \(\text{CuO}\) is reduced while \(\text{H}_2\) is oxidised in the same step, and the chapter therefore uses the single term **redox reaction**: 'Redox Reaction = Reduction + Oxidation'. The substance that brings about oxidation is the oxidant and the one that brings about reduction is the reductant.

The chapter also gives the wider, electron-based definitions that cover reactions with no oxygen or hydrogen in them at all: 'oxidation means losing one or more electrons', and 'When the positive charge on an atom or an ion increases or the negative charge on them decreases it is called oxidation, and when the positive charge decreases or the negative charge increases it is called reduction.'

**Similarity** — both are **exothermic**: heat is given out in each and the temperature of the mixture rises. The chapter names both. For sodium hydroxide: 'When the solid NaOH is dissolved in water heat is given out, and therefore the temperature increases', and it lists 'dissolution of sodium hydroxide in water' among its exothermic processes. For calcium oxide it prints

\(\text{CaO}(s) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{Ca(OH)}_2(aq) + \text{heat}\)   (Exothermic Reaction)

**Difference** — adding NaOH to water is only a **physical process** (dissolution), while adding CaO to water is a **chemical reaction**.

- No new substance is formed when sodium hydroxide dissolves; the composition of the matter does not change and the NaOH can in principle be recovered. The chapter draws exactly this contrast in its 'Use your brain power!' box — 'What is the difference in the process of dissolution and a chemical reaction? Does a new substance form when a solute dissolves in a solvent?' — and it defines a physical change as one in which 'the composition of matter remains the same'.
- Calcium oxide and water do not merely mix: 'Calcium hydroxide \((\text{Ca(OH)}_2)\) is formed by combination of calcium oxide and water with generation of large amount of heat.' A new substance with new bonds is formed, so this is a chemical change — and, being two reactants giving a single product, it is a combination reaction.

So the heat is common to both; what separates them is that one is a dissolution and the other a chemical reaction.

**Endothermic reaction** — a reaction in which heat is taken in. The chapter's wording is 'during endothermic chemical reactions heat is either absorbed from the surroundings or has to be supplied continuously from outside.'

**Example** — the decomposition of limestone, which the chapter itself labels an endothermic reaction:

\(\text{CaCO}_3(s) + \text{heat} \rightarrow \text{CaO}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g)\)   (Endothermic Reaction)

Calcium carbonate does not break up on its own; the test tube has to be heated strongly on a burner, and heating must go on for the reaction to continue. That is why the heat is written on the reactant side, or as the sign \(\Delta\) above the arrow — the chapter's convention for 'when heat is to be given from outside to bring about a reaction'.

The opposite case is an **exothermic** reaction, in which heat is given out and is written among the products, for example \(\text{CaO}(s) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{Ca(OH)}_2(aq) + \text{heat}\).

[Note: the chapter also distinguishes endothermic **processes** — physical changes such as melting of ice or dissolving potassium nitrate in water, where heat is absorbed but no new substance is formed — from endothermic **reactions** as defined above.]

**Combination reaction** — the chapter defines it as: 'When two or more reactants combine in a reaction to form a single product, it is a combination reaction.' The test is the number of products: however many reactants there are, exactly one product comes out.

**Examples**, all three from the chapter's own activities:

1. Ammonia gas and hydrogen chloride gas forming solid ammonium chloride, seen as white smoke —
\(\text{NH}_3(g) + \text{HCl}(g) \rightarrow \text{NH}_4\text{Cl}(s)\)

2. A burning magnesium ribbon forming a white powder of magnesium oxide —
\(2\text{Mg} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MgO}\)

3. Slaked lime formed from calcium oxide and water, with a large amount of heat —
\(\text{CaO} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Ca(OH)}_2 + \text{heat}\)

In each one, two reactants go in and a single product comes out.

**Balanced equation** — the chapter defines it from a count of atoms: 'the number of atoms of the elements in the reactants in this equation is same as the number of atoms of those elements in the products. Such an equation is called a balanced equation. If the number of atoms of each element is not the same on the two sides of an equation, it is called an unbalanced equation.'

The reason an equation must be balanced is the law of conservation of mass, which the chapter states as: 'In any reaction, the total mass of each of the elements in the reactants is same as the total mass of each of the respective elements in the products.'

**Example** — the chapter's own worked case. The unbalanced equation

\(\text{NaOH} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4 + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

has 1 Na on the left against 2 on the right and 3 H against 2, so it is unbalanced. Applying the factors 2 and 2 gives

\(2\text{NaOH} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

| Element | Atoms in reactants | Atoms in products |
|---|---|---|
| Na | 2 | 2 |
| O | 6 | 6 |
| H | 4 | 4 |
| S | 1 | 1 |

Every element now has the same number of atoms on both sides, so this is a balanced equation. Note the chapter's rule while balancing: 'the formula of a compound cannot be changed while balancing the number of atoms' — only factors may be placed in front of a formula.

**Displacement reaction** — the chapter's definition is: 'The reaction in which the place of the ion of a less reactive element in a compound is taken by another more reactive element by formation of its own ions, is called displacement reaction.'

**Example** — adding zinc dust to blue copper sulphate solution, the reaction the chapter opens with:

\(\text{CuSO}_4(aq) + \text{Zn}(s) \rightarrow \text{ZnSO}_4(aq) + \text{Cu}(s)\)

The chapter explains it in ionic terms: 'the \(\text{Zn}^{2+}\) ions formed from Zn atoms take the place of \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\) ions in copper sulphate, and Cu atoms, formed from \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\) ion come out. It means that Zn displaces Cu from \(\text{CuSO}_4\).' The blue colour of the copper sulphate solution fades to the colourless zinc sulphate solution, and copper particles settle out.

A second example from the chapter: iron displaces copper in the same way —

\(\text{CuSO}_4(aq) + \text{Fe}(s) \rightarrow \text{FeSO}_4(aq) + \text{Cu}(s)\)

The chapter notes that 'The elements iron and lead, similar to zinc, displace copper from its compound.'

Note how this differs from a **double displacement** reaction: here one element takes the place of another, whereas in a double displacement the ions of the two reactants are exchanged and a precipitate is formed.

The gas formed on heating limestone is **carbon dioxide**, and carbon dioxide is what turns lime water milky.

Limestone is calcium carbonate, and heating it strongly breaks it up — a decomposition reaction:

\(\text{CaCO}_3(s) \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{CaO}(s) + \text{CO}_2\uparrow\)

The chapter's activity is exactly this: calcium carbonate is heated in one test tube and the gas is led through a bent tube into freshly prepared lime water in a second test tube. 'We saw in the above activity that calcium carbonate undergoes decomposition reaction and the carbon dioxide gas formed turns the lime water milky. The second product of the reaction, the calcium oxide powder, remains behind in the first test tube.'

So the milkiness is not caused by heat or by the limestone itself; it is the test that identifies the gas coming over as \(\text{CO}_2\). Before heating, no gas is produced and the lime water stays clear — the chapter makes this point when discussing the effect of temperature on reaction rate: 'the lime water does not turn milky before heating the lime stone; because of the zero rate of reaction.'

[Note: the chapter states that carbon dioxide turns lime water milky and uses it as the test for \(\text{CO}_2\), but it does not print an equation for the reaction between carbon dioxide and lime water, so no equation for the milkiness itself is given here.]

Because the **rate of a reaction depends on the size of the reactant particles** — the smaller the particles, the faster the reaction.

Shahabad tile is a limestone tile, that is, calcium carbonate, and it reacts with hydrochloric acid to give off carbon dioxide. The chapter's activity takes equal weights of pieces and of powder of Shahabad tile in two test tubes and adds \(10\ \text{ml}\) of dilute HCl to each: 'the \(\text{CO}_2\) effervescence is formed slowly with the pieces of Shahabad tile while at a faster speed with the powder.'

The chapter draws the conclusion in the next sentence: 'The above observation indicates that the rate of a reaction depends upon the size of the particles of the reactants taking part in the reaction. Smaller the size of the reactant particles, higher is the rate of the reaction.'

The pieces present only their outer surface to the acid, so only a little of the tile is in contact with it at any moment and the tile takes a long time to disappear. Grinding the same weight into powder breaks it into a very large number of tiny particles, so far more of the tile is in contact with the acid at once, the reaction goes much faster, and the powder disappears rapidly.

The chapter uses the same effect elsewhere: 'It takes time for pieces of Shahabad tile to disappear in HCl' is the same observation as its earlier note that staining of a Shahabad tile by lemon juice is a chemical change.

Because **the dilution of concentrated sulphuric acid with water is strongly exothermic**, and adding the acid slowly to water with stirring is the only safe order.

The chapter states the danger and the remedy together: 'In the process of dilution of concentrated sulphuric acid with water, very large amount of heat is liberated. As a result, water gets evaporated instantaneously, if it is poured in to the concentrated sulphuric acid, which may cause an accident. To avoid this, required amount of water is taken in a glass container and small quantity of concentrated sulphuric acid at a time is added with stirring. Therefore, only a small amount of heat is liberated at a time.'

So the two rules follow from one another:

- **acid into water, not water into acid** — if water is poured into the concentrated acid, the small amount of water meets a large amount of acid, is heated far past its boiling point at once and flashes into steam, throwing corrosive acid out of the container;
- **slowly, with constant stirring** — adding a small quantity at a time releases only a small amount of heat at a time, and stirring spreads that heat through the whole of the water instead of letting it build up at one spot.

The large volume of water present also absorbs the heat and keeps the temperature of the mixture from rising sharply.

Because oil kept in the open **undergoes air oxidation and turns rancid**, and an air tight container keeps the air away from it.

The chapter describes the change: 'When we use old, left over cooking oil for making food stuff, it is found to have foul odour called rancidity. If food is cooked in such oil, its taste also changes. When oil or ghee is left aside for a long time or fried food is left aside for a long time it undergoes air oxidation and becomes rancid.'

So the spoiling is a slow oxidation reaction between the oil and the oxygen of the air, and it damages both the smell and the taste of the oil and of anything cooked in it. Cutting off the supply of oxygen slows that reaction down, which is why the chapter says: 'The process of oxidation reaction of food stuff can also be slowed down by storing it in air tight container.'

The chapter gives one other way of preventing it: 'Rancidity in the food stuff cooked in oil or ghee is prevented by using antioxidants.'

The picture shows the **rusting of iron**, and it makes the point that rusting is not a simple reaction of oxygen with the iron surface but an **electrochemical reaction**. The chapter says so: 'The rust on iron does not form by a simple reaction of oxygen with iron surface. The rust is formed by an electrochemical reaction. Different regions on the surface of iron become anode and cathode.'

In the picture a drop of water is lying on an iron surface. The part of the iron under the drop is marked **anode**, the part outside it — where the collected rust is sitting — is marked **cathode**, and an arrow marked \(e^-\) shows electrons travelling through the metal from the anode region to the cathode region.

**1. At the anode region, iron is oxidised.** Iron atoms give up two electrons each and pass into the water drop as \(\text{Fe}^{2+}\) ions — the picture marks these as \(\text{Fe}^{2+}(aq)\) leaving the surface:

\(\text{Fe}(s) \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{2+}(aq) + 2e^-\)

**2. At the cathode region, oxygen from the air is reduced.** The electrons released by the iron travel through the metal to this region, where they are taken up by dissolved oxygen. The picture gives two forms of this half-reaction, one in acidic conditions and one in neutral or alkaline conditions:

\(\text{O}_2(g) + 4\text{H}^+(aq) + 4e^- \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\)

\(\text{O}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + 4e^- \rightarrow 4\text{OH}^-\)

**3. The rust itself.** 'When \(\text{Fe}^{2+}\) ions migrate from the anode region they react with water and further get oxidised to form \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) ions. A reddish coloured hydrated oxide is formed from \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) ions. It is called rust. It collects on the surface.'

\(2\text{Fe}^{3+}(aq) + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3\cdot\text{H}_2\text{O}(s) + 6\text{H}^+(aq)\)

This is the reddish brown solid labelled 'Collected rust' in the picture, with its formula \(\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3\cdot\text{H}_2\text{O}\) written beside it.

Both water and air are needed, which is why the rust forms where the water drop meets the iron and the air: the chapter's four-test-tube activity shows that 'Both water and air are necessary for rusting. The rusting process takes place rapidly in presence of a salt.'

Rusting is therefore a redox reaction — iron is oxidised, oxygen is reduced — and it is an example of **corrosion**: 'Due to various components of atmosphere, oxidation of metals takes place, consequently resulting in their damage. This is called corrosion.'

[Note: the chapter writes the general formula of rust as \(\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3\cdot X\,\text{H}_2\text{O}\) in its prose, because the number of water molecules attached is variable, while its equation (29) and this picture both write the single hydrate \(\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3\cdot\text{H}_2\text{O}\). Equation (29) is balanced as printed with the monohydrate. The half-reaction giving \(4\text{OH}^-\) appears only in this picture; the chapter's prose gives only the half-reaction giving water.]

\(\text{Fe} + \text{S} \rightarrow \text{FeS}\)

- **Iron (Fe) is oxidised.**
- **Sulphur (S) is reduced.**

Neither oxygen nor hydrogen appears anywhere in this reaction, so the chapter's oxygen-and-hydrogen definitions cannot be applied to it. The wider definition has to be used — the one the chapter gives in terms of electrons and charge: 'oxidation means losing one or more electrons', and 'When the positive charge on an atom or an ion increases or the negative charge on them decreases it is called oxidation, and when the positive charge decreases or the negative charge increases it is called reduction.'

Ferrous sulphide is an ionic compound built from \(\text{Fe}^{2+}\) and \(\text{S}^{2-}\). Each iron atom gives up two electrons, so its charge rises from \(0\) to \(+2\) — iron is oxidised. Each sulphur atom takes up those two electrons, so its charge falls from \(0\) to \(-2\) — sulphur is reduced. Iron is the reductant and sulphur the oxidant, and as always the two changes happen together, making this a redox reaction.

[Note: the chapter gives the electron and charge definitions used here, but it does not itself state the charges carried by iron and sulphur in FeS.]

\(2\text{Ag}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 4\,\text{Ag} + \text{O}_2\uparrow\)

This item has only **one** reactant, silver oxide, so oxidation and reduction cannot be shared between two different reactants — both changes take place inside \(\text{Ag}_2\text{O}\) itself:

- **Silver oxide is reduced**, because it loses its oxygen. The chapter's rule is 'the reaction in which a reactant loses oxygen to form the product is also called reduction reaction'. In terms of charge, silver goes from \(\text{Ag}^{+}\) in the oxide to \(\text{Ag}\) metal, so its positive charge decreases — reduction.
- **The oxide part of the same reactant is oxidised**, because the \(\text{O}^{2-}\) ions give up their electrons and come off as neutral oxygen gas. Their negative charge decreases, which by the chapter's rule 'the negative charge on them decreases it is called oxidation' is oxidation.

So \(\text{Ag}_2\text{O}\) is the reactant that undergoes reduction, and the oxygen within it is what undergoes oxidation. This is a decomposition reaction — one reactant giving two products — and it is a redox reaction in which one substance is both oxidised and reduced.

[Note: the question asks for 'the reactants that undergo oxidation and reduction', which reads as though two different reactants are expected. Only this item of Q.6 has a single reactant, so the two changes have to be located inside it. The chapter itself never works an example of this kind.]

\(2\text{Mg} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MgO}\)

- **Magnesium (Mg) is oxidised.**
- **Oxygen (\(\text{O}_2\)) is reduced.**

The chapter prints this very equation as its first illustration of oxidation and states the rule it illustrates: 'The chemical reaction in which a reactant combines with oxygen or loses hydrogen to form the product is called oxidation reaction.' Magnesium combines with oxygen to form magnesium oxide, so magnesium is oxidised. The chapter's activity is a magnesium strip held in tongs and ignited: 'On burning in air a white powder of magnesium oxide is formed.'

Oxygen is the reactant reduced. Magnesium oxide is ionic, built from \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\) and \(\text{O}^{2-}\): each magnesium atom loses two electrons (charge \(0 \rightarrow +2\), oxidation) and each oxygen atom gains two (charge \(0 \rightarrow -2\), reduction, since 'the negative charge increases it is called reduction'). Magnesium is the reductant and oxygen the oxidant.

The same reaction is also a combination reaction, since two reactants give a single product.

\(\text{NiO} + \text{H}_2 \rightarrow \text{Ni} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

- **Nickel oxide (NiO) is reduced.**
- **Hydrogen (\(\text{H}_2\)) is oxidised.**

This is the same pattern as the chapter's worked example \(\text{CuO} + \text{H}_2 \rightarrow \text{Cu} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\), which it explains as: 'an oxygen atom goes away from CuO (copper oxide), which means that reduction of copper oxide takes place, whereas hydrogen molecule takes up oxygen atom and water \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) is formed meaning, oxidation of hydrogen takes place.'

Applying the same two rules here — 'the reaction in which a reactant loses oxygen to form the product is also called reduction reaction', and 'a reactant combines with oxygen ... is called oxidation reaction' — nickel oxide loses its oxygen and is reduced to nickel metal, while hydrogen takes up that oxygen and is oxidised to water. Hydrogen is the reductant and nickel oxide the oxidant, and since both changes happen in the same step it is a redox reaction.

\(\text{H}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_7(l) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(l)\)

**Step I** — the equation as given.

**Step II** — count the atoms on both sides.

| Element | Atoms in reactants | Atoms in products |
|---|---|---|
| H | 4 | 2 |
| S | 2 | 1 |
| O | 8 | 4 |

The numbers do not match, so the equation is unbalanced.

**Step III** — begin with the compound holding the greatest number of atoms, \(\text{H}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_7\) (11 atoms), and with an element in it whose numbers are unequal on the two sides. Sulphur is 2 on the left and 1 on the right. The formula of a compound may not be changed, so a factor of 2 is applied to \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\):

\(\text{H}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_7 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\)

**Step IV** — check again.

| Element | Atoms in reactants | Atoms in products |
|---|---|---|
| H | 4 | 4 |
| S | 2 | 2 |
| O | 8 | 8 |

Every element is now equal on both sides, so the balanced equation is

\(\text{H}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_7(l) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(l)\)

\(\text{SO}_2(g) + \text{H}_2\text{S}(aq) \rightarrow \text{S}(s) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\)

**Step I** — the equation as given.

**Step II** — count the atoms.

| Element | Atoms in reactants | Atoms in products |
|---|---|---|
| S | 2 | 1 |
| H | 2 | 2 |
| O | 2 | 1 |

Unbalanced.

**Step III** — take oxygen first, since it needs the smaller factor. Oxygen is 2 on the left and 1 on the right, so apply a factor of 2 to \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\):

\(\text{SO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{S} \rightarrow \text{S} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

Hydrogen has now gone out of balance — 2 on the left, 4 on the right — so apply a factor of 2 to \(\text{H}_2\text{S}\):

\(\text{SO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{S} \rightarrow \text{S} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

Sulphur is now 3 on the left (one in \(\text{SO}_2\), two in \(2\text{H}_2\text{S}\)) against 1 on the right, so apply a factor of 3 to S:

\(\text{SO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{S} \rightarrow 3\text{S} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

**Step IV** — check.

| Element | Atoms in reactants | Atoms in products |
|---|---|---|
| S | 3 | 3 |
| H | 4 | 4 |
| O | 2 | 2 |

Balanced, so the final equation is

\(\text{SO}_2(g) + 2\text{H}_2\text{S}(aq) \rightarrow 3\text{S}(s) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\)

This agrees with the chapter, which prints the same reaction as \(2\text{H}_2\text{S} + \text{SO}_2 \rightarrow 3\text{S} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\) among its examples of redox reactions.

\(\text{Ag}(s) + \text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgCl}\downarrow + \text{H}_2\uparrow\)

**Step I** — the equation as given.

**Step II** — count the atoms.

| Element | Atoms in reactants | Atoms in products |
|---|---|---|
| Ag | 1 | 1 |
| H | 1 | 2 |
| Cl | 1 | 1 |

Hydrogen is unequal, so the equation is unbalanced.

**Step III** — balance hydrogen by applying a factor of 2 to HCl:

\(\text{Ag} + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{AgCl} + \text{H}_2\)

Chlorine is now 2 on the left against 1 on the right, so apply a factor of 2 to AgCl:

\(\text{Ag} + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow 2\text{AgCl} + \text{H}_2\)

Silver is now 1 on the left against 2 on the right, so apply a factor of 2 to Ag:

\(2\text{Ag} + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow 2\text{AgCl} + \text{H}_2\)

**Step IV** — check.

| Element | Atoms in reactants | Atoms in products |
|---|---|---|
| Ag | 2 | 2 |
| H | 2 | 2 |
| Cl | 2 | 2 |

Balanced, so the final equation is

\(2\text{Ag}(s) + 2\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow 2\text{AgCl}\downarrow + \text{H}_2\uparrow\)

This is the form the chapter itself prints for this reaction earlier in the chapter, where it asks for the physical states of the reactants and products.

\(\text{NaOH}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\)

This is the equation the chapter balances step by step as its worked example, so the same four steps are followed here.

**Step I** — write the equation from the word equation 'Sodium hydroxide + Sulphuric acid \(\rightarrow\) Sodium sulphate + water'.

**Step II** — count the atoms.

| Element | Atoms in reactants | Atoms in products |
|---|---|---|
| Na | 1 | 2 |
| O | 5 | 5 |
| H | 3 | 2 |
| S | 1 | 1 |

Sodium and hydrogen are unequal, so the equation is unbalanced.

**Step III** — 'It is convenient to start balancing an equation from the compound which contains the maximum number of atoms.' \(\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4\) and \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\) each hold seven atoms; take \(\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4\), and within it sodium, which is 1 on the left and 2 on the right. The formula NaOH cannot be rewritten as \(\text{Na}_2\text{OH}\), so a factor of 2 is applied to NaOH instead:

\(2\text{NaOH} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4 + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

Now hydrogen (4 against 2) and oxygen (6 against 5) are unequal. Balance hydrogen first, 'as it requires a smaller factor' — apply a factor of 2 to \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\):

\(2\text{NaOH} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

**Step IV** — check and write the final equation.

| Element | Atoms in reactants | Atoms in products |
|---|---|---|
| Na | 2 | 2 |
| O | 6 | 6 |
| H | 4 | 4 |
| S | 1 | 1 |

All four elements are equal on both sides, so the balanced equation is

\(2\text{NaOH}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\)

Balancing oxygen was never needed separately — it came right on its own once sodium and hydrogen had been balanced.

\(\text{HCl} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{heat}\)

**Exothermic reaction.**

Heat is written on the product side, which by the chapter's rule means it is given out as the reactants change into the products: 'During exothermic chemical reactions heat is given away when reactants are transformed into the products.' The temperature of the mixture therefore rises. This is the neutralisation of hydrochloric acid by sodium hydroxide, and it needs no heating from outside to make it go.

\(2\text{KClO}_3(s) \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\text{KCl}(s) + 3\text{O}_2\uparrow\)

**Endothermic reaction.**

The sign \(\Delta\) is written above the arrow, and the chapter's convention for that is explicit: 'When heat is to be given from outside to bring about a reaction, it is indicated by the sign \(\Delta\) written above the arrow that indicates the direction of the reaction.' Heat has to be supplied for the reaction to happen at all, which by the chapter's definition — 'during endothermic chemical reactions heat is either absorbed from the surroundings or has to be supplied continuously from outside' — makes it endothermic.

The chapter uses this same reaction when discussing catalysts: 'On heating potassium chlorate \((\text{KClO}_3)\) decomposes slowly', and it decomposes rapidly in the presence of manganese dioxide. It is also a decomposition reaction, since one reactant gives two products.

\(\text{CaO} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Ca(OH)}_2 + \text{heat}\)

**Exothermic reaction.**

The chapter labels this exact equation an exothermic reaction, and describes the activity behind it: 'Calcium hydroxide \((\text{Ca(OH)}_2)\) is formed by combination of calcium oxide and water with generation of large amount of heat.' Heat appears among the products, so it is given out and the water in the beaker becomes hot. It is also a combination reaction, since two reactants give a single product.

\(\text{CaCO}_3(s) \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{CaO}(s) + \text{CO}_2\uparrow\)

**Endothermic reaction.**

The chapter labels this exact reaction an endothermic reaction, writing it as \(\text{CaCO}_3(s) + \text{heat} \rightarrow \text{CaO}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g)\) — that is, with the heat on the reactant side, taken in rather than given out. Here the same thing is shown by the \(\Delta\) above the arrow, the chapter's sign for heat supplied from outside.

The chapter's activity confirms it: the limestone has to be heated strongly on a burner before any carbon dioxide comes off, and 'the lime water does not turn milky before heating the lime stone; because of the zero rate of reaction.' It is also a decomposition reaction, one reactant giving two products.

| Reactants | Products | Type of chemical reaction |
|---|---|---|
| \(\text{BaCl}_2(aq) + \text{ZnSO}_4(aq)\) | \(\text{BaSO}_4\downarrow + \text{ZnCl}_2(aq)\) | Double displacement |
| \(2\text{AgCl}(s)\) | \(2\text{Ag}(s) + \text{Cl}_2(g)\) | Decomposition |
| \(\text{CuSO}_4(aq) + \text{Fe}(s)\) | \(\text{FeSO}_4(aq) + \text{Cu}(s)\) | Displacement |
| \(\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) + \text{CO}_2(g)\) | \(\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3(aq)\) | Combination |

**Why each row goes where it does**

1. \(\text{BaCl}_2(aq) + \text{ZnSO}_4(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4\downarrow + \text{ZnCl}_2(aq)\) — the barium and zinc ions exchange their partners and an insoluble white solid separates out, which is the chapter's definition of a **double displacement** reaction: 'The reaction in which the ions in the reactants are exchanged to form a precipitate is a double displacement reaction.'

2. \(2\text{AgCl}(s) \rightarrow 2\text{Ag}(s) + \text{Cl}_2(g)\) — a single reactant gives two products, which is **decomposition**: 'The chemical reaction in which two or more products are formed from a single reactant is a Decomposition reaction.'

3. \(\text{CuSO}_4(aq) + \text{Fe}(s) \rightarrow \text{FeSO}_4(aq) + \text{Cu}(s)\) — iron, the more reactive element, takes the place of copper in copper sulphate and copper comes out, which is **displacement**. This is one of the two reactions the chapter sets in its own 'Use your brain power!' box on displacement, and it notes that 'The elements iron and lead, similar to zinc, displace copper from its compound.'

4. \(\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) + \text{CO}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3(aq)\) — two reactants give a single product, which is **combination**: 'When two or more reactants combine in a reaction to form a single product, it is a combination reaction.'
